Benchmark.title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
Benchmark.description: All CIS Benchmarks ™ (Benchmarks) focus on technical configuration settings used to maintain and/or increase the security of the addressed technology, and they should be used in conjunction with other essential cyber hygiene tasks like: • Monitoring the base operating system and applications for vulnerabilities and quickly updating with the latest security patches. • End-point protection (Antivirus software, Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR), etc.). • Logging and monitoring user and system activity. In the end, the Benchmarks are designed to be a key component of a comprehensive cybersecurity program. Important Usage Information All Benchmarks are available free for non-commercial use from the CIS Website. They can be used to manually assess and remediate systems and applications. In lieu of manual assessment and remediation, there are several tools available to assist with assessment: • CIS Configuration Assessment Tool (CIS-CAT ® Pro Assessor) • CIS Benchmarks ™ Certified 3rd Party Tooling These tools make the hardening process much more scalable for large numbers of systems and applications. NOTE: Some tooling focuses only on the Benchmark Recommendations that can be fully automated (skipping ones marked Manual). It is important that ALL Recommendations ( Automated and Manual) be addressed since all are important for properly securing systems and are typically in scope for audits. Key Stakeholders Cybersecurity is a collaborative effort, and cross functional cooperation is imperative within an organization to discuss, test, and deploy Benchmarks in an effective and efficient way. The Benchmarks are developed to be best practice configuration guidelines applicable to a wide range of use cases. In some organizations, exceptions to specific Recommendations will be needed, and this team should work to prioritize the problematic Recommendations based on several factors like risk, time, cost, and labor. These exceptions should be properly categorized and documented for auditing purposes. Apply the Correct Version of a Benchmark Benchmarks are developed and tested for a specific set of products and versions and applying an incorrect Benchmark to a system can cause the resulting pass/fail score to be incorrect. This is due to the assessment of settings that do not apply to the target systems. To assure the correct Benchmark is being assessed: • Deploy the Benchmark applicable to the way settings are managed in the environment: An example of this is the Microsoft Windows family of Benchmarks, which have separate Benchmarks for Group Policy, Intune, and Stand-alone systems based upon how system management is deployed. Applying the wrong Benchmark in this case will give invalid results. • Use the most recent version of a Benchmark: This is true for all Benchmarks, but especially true for cloud technologies. Cloud technologies change frequently and using an older version of a Benchmark may have invalid methods for auditing and remediation. Exceptions The guidance items in the Benchmarks are called recommendations and not requirements, and exceptions to some of them are expected and acceptable. The Benchmarks strive to be a secure baseline, or starting point, for a specific technology, with known issues identified during Benchmark development are documented in the Impact section of each Recommendation. In addition, organizational, system specific requirements, or local site policy may require changes as well, or an exception to a Recommendation or group of Recommendations (e.g. A Benchmark could Recommend that a Web server not be installed on the system, but if a system's primary purpose is to function as a Webserver, there should be a documented exception to this Recommendation for that specific server). In the end, exceptions to some Benchmark Recommendations are common and acceptable, and should be handled as follows: • The reasons for the exception should be reviewed cross-functionally and be well documented for audit purposes. • A plan should be developed for mitigating, or eliminating, the exception in the future, if applicable. • If the organization decides to accept the risk of this exception (not work toward mitigation or elimination), this should be documented for audit purposes. It is the responsibility of the organization to determine their overall security policy, and which settings are applicable to their unique needs based on the overall risk profile for the organization. Remediation CIS has developed Build Kits for many technologies to assist in the automation of hardening systems. Build Kits are designed to correspond to Benchmark's “Remediation” section, which provides the manual remediation steps necessary to make that Recommendation compliant to the Benchmark. When remediating systems (changing configuration settings on deployed systems as per the Benchmark's Recommendations), please approach this with caution and test thoroughly. The following is a reasonable remediation approach to follow: • CIS Build Kits, or internally developed remediation methods should never be applied to production systems without proper testing. • Proper testing consists of the following: o Understand the configuration (including installed applications) of the targeted systems. Various parts of the organization may need different configurations (e.g., software developers vs standard office workers). o Read the Impact section of the given Recommendation to help determine if there might be an issue with the targeted systems. o Test the configuration changes with representative lab system(s). If issues arise during testing, they can be resolved prior to deploying to any production systems. o When testing is complete, initially deploy to a small sub-set of production systems and monitor closely for issues. If there are issues, they can be resolved prior to deploying more broadly. o When the initial deployment above is completes successfully, iteratively deploy to additional systems and monitor closely for issues. Repeat this process until the full deployment is complete. Summary Using the Benchmarks Certified tools, working as a team with key stakeholders, being selective with exceptions, and being careful with remediation deployment, it is possible to harden large numbers of deployed systems in a cost effective, efficient, and safe manner. NOTE: As previously stated, the PDF versions of the CIS Benchmarks ™ are available for free, non-commercial use on the CIS Website. All other formats of the CIS Benchmarks ™ (MS Word, Excel, and Build Kits) are available for CIS SecureSuite ® members. CIS-CAT ® Pro is also available to CIS SecureSuite ® members. Target Technology Details This document, CIS (Center for Internet Security) Oracle SaaS Foundations benchmark, provides prescriptive guidance for establishing a secure baseline configuration for Oracle SaaS environments. The scope of this benchmark is to establish a base level of security for organizations utilizing the included Oracle SaaS applications. The benchmark is not an exhaustive list of all possible security configurations and architectures. The benchmark should be taken as a starting point and tailored as appropriate to meet site-specific needs. This benchmark covers Oracle Fusion and EPM SaaS Applications where explicitly highlighted, and will be extended to other Oracle SaaS applications in future releases. Additionally, Oracle SaaS applications are associated with an Oracle Cloud Infrastructure tenancy. Therefore, organizations should also leverage the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Foundations Benchmark to establish a secure baseline configuration for their OCI tenancy running Oracle SaaS.

Rule.title: Ensure Password Policy Enforces Length and Rotation
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>A strong password policy helps protect Oracle Fusion and EPM SaaS environments against unauthorized access by enforcing minimum standards for password length, rotation, and reuse prevention for both user and administrative accounts.
Administrators can configure password policies in:
• Fusion SaaS (pre-upgrade environments): Security Console Administration Password Policy
• Fusion SaaS (upgraded environments) and Oracle EPM: OCI IAM Identity Domain Console Recommended Configuration:
• Require passwords to be at least 14 characters in length.
• Prevent reuse of the last five passwords.
• Require administrative passwords to expire and be changed at least every 365 days.
• Lock accounts after five failed login attempts.
These parameters are available and enforceable in both pre-upgrade and post-upgrade identity configurations across Oracle Fusion and EPM SaaS applications.

Rationale:
Enforcing password length and rotation reduces the likelihood that weak or compromised passwords are exploited to gain unauthorized access.
Overly frequent password changes can lead to insecure workarounds such as predictable patterns or insecure storage. Use of longer password utilizing passphrases should be encouraged to make passwords easier for users to remember. Balance password policy strictness with usability, and complement with multi-factor authentication (MFA) to minimize reliance on passwords alone.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
Pre-upgrade (Security Console):
1. Navigate to Navigator Tools, Security Console, Administration, Password Policy.
2. Configure the following values:
• Minimum Length: 14
• Require Numbers: No
• Require Special Characters: No
• Password Expiration (Days): 365
• Prevent Reuse of Last Passwords: 5
• Failed Sign-In Attempts Before Lockout: 5 3. Save and communicate changes to all users.
EPM & Post-upgrade (OCI IAM Identity Domain):
1. In the OCI Console, open the Identity Domain Security, Password Policy.
2. Configure equivalent parameters for length, complexity, expiration, reuse prevention, and lockout.
3. Save policy updates; they take immediate effect for all users.

check.check-content:
For pre-upgrade environments:
1. Sign in as a Security Administrator or IT Security Manager.
2. Navigate to Tools, Security Console, Administration, Password Policy.
3. Verify that:
• Minimum length is ≥ 14 characters.
• Password expiration is ≤ 365 days.
• Password reuse prevention is ≥ 5 previous passwords.
• Account lockout triggers after ≤ 5 failed login attempts.
For EPM and post-upgrade environments (OCI IAM Identity Domain):
1. In the OCI Console, go to Identity & Security, Domains, Security, Password Policy.
2. Confirm the equivalent settings:
• Minimum length ≥ 14.
• Expiration ≤ 365 days.
• Password history ≥ 5.
• Account lockout ≤ 5 failed attempts.
3. Ensure lockout duration and auto-unlock timing meet organizational requirements.

Rule.title: Ensure MFA is Enforced for All SaaS Users
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) requires users to present an additional verification factor beyond username and password. In Oracle Fusion environments, native MFA enforcement via Identity Domain sign- on policies functions only after the environment’s identity service is upgraded to OCI IAM. For environments not yet upgraded, MFA must remain delegated to an external IdP or await the identity upgrade. Where supported, phishing-resistant factors (for example, FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys or hardware security keys) are preferred over SMS or email OTP.

Rationale:
MFA protects against credential theft and password reuse attacks. Enforcing MFA across all SaaS users - whether they authenticate through the Fusion Identity Domain, an external OCI IAM domain, or another IdP — provides consistent protection and centralized policy control.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. If the Fusion environment is upgraded to OCI IAM:
• In Fusion Security Console User Categories, Two-Factor Authentication, enable MFA for all categories.
2. If the environment is not upgraded or uses a federated IdP:
• Enable MFA in the external IdP or external OCI IAM domain and ensure it applies to all users accessing Fusion.
3. Communicate enrollment instructions and verify MFA enrollment via Fusion My Profile, Manage Secure Verification.
4. Perform test logins to confirm MFA prompts are consistently applied.

check.check-content:
1. Check if the Fusion environment is upgraded to OCI IAM or uses an external IdP.
2. If on OCI IAM, review Security Console, User Categories, Two-Factor Authentication and confirm all user categories have MFA enabled.
3. If identity upgrade is not yet performed, verify that MFA is enforced via the external IdP for all users.
4. Test login with a standard SaaS user account and confirm MFA is required (native or via IdP).

Rule.title: Ensure Phishing-Resistant MFA Is Enforced for SaaS Administrators and Privileged Accounts
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) requires users to present an additional verification factor beyond username and password. In Oracle Fusion environments, native MFA enforcement via Identity Domain sign- on policies functions only after the environment’s identity service is upgraded to OCI IAM or an external IdP. For environments not yet upgraded, MFA must be delegated to an external IdP or await the identity upgrade.
SaaS Administrators and other SaaS privileged accounts must authenticate using phishing-resistant MFA methods such as FIDO2/WebAuthn security keys, platform passkeys, or passwordless authentication. Weaker factors such as SMS OTP or email OTP should be disabled for administrative and privileged accounts.

Rationale:
Privileged accounts are high-value targets. Enforcing MFA with phishing resistant factors reduces the risk of unauthorized administrative access even if credentials are compromised. To use native MFA, the identity service must be on OCI IAM, which provides the required support for enforcing sign-on policies and MFA natively.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. If identity upgrade is not finalized implement MFA via the external IdP.
2. After the upgrade, in the Security Console open User Categories Two-Factor Authentication and enable MFA for administrator/privileged categories.
3. Define valid phishing resistant MFA factors (mobile authenticator, FIDO, etc.).
4. Save settings and ensure SaaS users enroll in MFA during their next login.
5. Test that privileged accounts require MFA (OCI IAM) and fallback to IdP enrollment where needed.

check.check-content:
1. Determine if the Fusion environment has been upgraded to use OCI IAM (check Fusion environment’s maintenance/upgrade status) or is using an external IdP for MFA.
2. Access the Security Console User Categories Two-Factor Authentication and confirm SaaS administrators/privileged categories have MFA enabled. Only enable factors that are considered phishing resistant.
3. If identity upgrade has not occurred, verify that MFA is enforced via the external IdP for privileged accounts.
4. Test login with a privileged account and confirm MFA prompt is required (native or via IdP).

Rule.title: Ensure Fusion Applications Administrators Have Access Only to Fusion Applications Resources
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that Fusion Applications Administrators are granted Console access only to Fusion Applications resources. Their IAM policies must be scoped exclusively to the fusion-applications-family resource type, without granting access to other OCI services.

Rationale:
Fusion Applications Administrators are responsible for managing SaaS environments, not the broader OCI infrastructure. Granting them access to additional OCI services (for example, Compute, Networking, Object Storage) is unnecessary and increases the attack surface. Restricting their access to Fusion Applications resources enforces least privilege, reduces risk of accidental or malicious changes to unrelated services, and aligns with compliance requirements for segregation of duties.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. Identify the group(s) used for Fusion Applications Administrators (e.g., FusionAdmins).
2. Remove any existing policies that provide access to non-Fusion OCI services.
3. Create or update the policy to restrict privileges to Fusion Applications only:
• For administrators:
Allow group FusionAdmins to manage fusion-applications-family in tenancy
• For read-only roles (if needed):
Allow group FusionViewers to read fusion-applications-family in tenancy

check.check-content:
1. Navigate to Identity & Security Policies.
2. Review policies attached to groups containing Fusion Applications Administrators.
3. Confirm that:
• Policies use the fusion-applications-family resource type.
• No broad tenancy-wide permissions (such as manage all-resources or unrelated service resource types) are present.
4. Verify that Console access for Fusion Administrators shows only Fusion Applications in the navigation menu.

Rule.title: Ensure OCI Console Access Is Restricted to Administrative Accounts
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that only designated administrative accounts are allowed to log in to the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Console. All non-admin user accounts must have the console password capability disabled, and sign-on policies must restrict Console application access to administrative groups only.

Rationale:
The OCI Console provides broad administrative access. Restricting console login exclusively to administrative accounts minimizes the risk of unauthorized changes and reduces the attack surface in case of credential compromise. Non-administrative users can still interact with OCI through APIs, SDKs, or federated identity providers without requiring console access.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. For each non-admin user:
• Navigate to Identity & Security Domains Edit User Capabilities.
• Uncheck Can use Console password.
• Save changes.
2. Update the Sign-On Policy for the identity domain:
• Add a rule that allows Console login only for users in an Admin group.
• Add a default deny rule for all other users.
3. Test the configuration by attempting Console login with both an admin and a non- admin account.

check.check-content:
1. Navigate to Identity & Security Domains Users.
• For each non-admin user, confirm that Can use Console password is unchecked under Edit User Capabilities.
2. Navigate to Domains Security Sign-On Policies.
• Verify there is a policy rule that allows Console access only for designated administrative groups.
• Confirm that a deny rule is in place for all other users.

Rule.title: Ensure Privileged and Administrative Roles Are Restricted to Known IP Addresses
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>When Location-Based Access Control (LBAC) is enabled in Oracle Fusion Applications, administrative and privileged roles must not be configured for unrestricted access. In the Fusion Security Console, privileged roles such as IT Security Manager and Application Implementation Consultant include the option “Enable Role for Access from All IP Addresses.” This setting should remain disabled, ensuring these roles can only be accessed from known and approved IP ranges defined within the LBAC configuration or associated network perimeter.

Rationale:
Restricting administrative and privileged access to known IP ranges prevents unauthorized or high-risk logins from untrusted networks. This measure reduces the attack surface for high-privilege accounts and aligns with the principle of least privilege by ensuring elevated functions are only available from managed corporate networks or approved secure endpoints.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. Sign in to Fusion Security Console with an administrative account.
2. Navigate to Roles, Search, IT Security Manager (or equivalent privileged roles).
3. Go to the Administration tab and ensure the checkbox Enable Role for Access from All IP Addresses is cleared.
4. Verify that the role is correctly assigned to the appropriate network perimeter under LBAC settings, restricting access to known IP ranges.
5. Test access from a trusted IP and confirm the role remains functional; test from an unapproved IP to confirm access is denied.

check.check-content:
1. Confirm that LBAC is enabled for the Fusion environment.
2. Sign in to Fusion Security Console with appropriate privileges.
3. Navigate to Roles, Search, IT Security Manager (and other privileged roles).
4. Open the role and go to the Administration tab.
5. Verify that the checkbox Enable Role for Access from All IP Addresses is not selected.
6. Confirm that privileged roles are associated with the intended network perimeter or known IP range within LBAC configuration.

Rule.title: Ensure Privileged Access is Certified Periodically
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The purpose of this recommendation is to ensure that only authorized users retain elevated access, by reviewing users' abilities periodically - monthly for IT administrators and quarterly for others.

Rationale:
Users could accumulate roles and data access as their responsibilities change, giving them elevated or unintended abilities that they could use erroneously or maliciously with substantial impact on operations and finances.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
When a role should be removed from a user either:
• Remove unwanted role.
• Leave role and monitor the transactions performed by the user (see below).
1. Review the user's actions since the previous review:
Manual method:
1. Navigate to Tools Reports and Analytics.
2. Select the appropriate dashboards or reports.
3. Review the transactions that the role allows.
Automated method: 1.Create Transaction Controls in Fusion Cloud Applications Risk Management that continuously monitor those transactions and initiate investigation workflows when unwanted activity occurs.
1. Deploy the appropriate controls using the instructions in Continuously Monitor Transactions.

check.check-content:
Review users' abilities Manual method:
1. Navigate to Tools Scheduled Processes 2. Review User and Role Access Audit Report and User Role Membership Report (or schedule them, then review them).
Automated method:
1. Initiate one or more Access Certification campaigns in Fusion Cloud Applications Risk Management using the instructions in Digitize Access Certification Workflows.
2. For example, initiate campaigns to review users with unauthorized access; detect privilege creep (accumulation of access no longer required); or detect users, organizations or roles recently added or not included in the reviews.

Rule.title: Ensure Oracle Break Glass for Fusion Cloud Service Is Enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Oracle Break Glass for Fusion Cloud Service provides a customer-controlled workflow that governs Oracle personnel’s emergency access to the Fusion Cloud database and middleware tiers. When enabled, Oracle cannot access customer data without explicit approval from your designated administrators for each one-off service activity.

Rationale:
Activating and monitoring the Break Glass service ensures that privileged Oracle support access occurs only under strict governance, audit logging, and time-bound approvals, reducing insider and third-party access risk.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
In console:
1. Activate Break Glass service via Oracle Cloud Subscription management.
2. Define approvers (Fusion Cloud Administrators).
3. Enable notifications for Break Glass request/approval activities.
4. Enable post-access revocation and audit logs are retained

check.check-content:
In console:
1. Go to: Access Oracle Cloud Console 2. Select My Services → Subscriptions → Fusion Cloud Service 3. Verify that Break Glass status is Enabled 4. Verify that designated approvers are defined in the workflow 5. Verify that post-access revocation and audit logs are retained

Rule.title: Ensure Basic Authentication Is Blocked for SOAP and REST API Integrations
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Organizations must block the use of Basic Authentication for all SOAP and REST API integrations with Oracle SaaS Applications. This can be achieved by disabling Basic Authentication at the Fusion Applications layer and enforcing OAuth 2.0 as the only supported authentication method. Automated monitoring of Fusion audit logs and OCI IAM authentication logs should also be configured to detect and alert on attempted Basic Authentication use.

Rationale:
Blocking Basic Authentication prevents insecure clients from connecting, even if misconfigured. Combined with monitoring, this ensures that only OAuth tokens are accepted, reducing exposure to replay attacks, credential theft, and non-compliant integrations.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. Submit a Service Request to Oracle SaaS Operations asking to disable Basic Authentication for APIs in your Fusion instance.
2. Include details of your current integrations (endpoints, methods) that rely on Basic Auth.
3. Confirm with Oracle that Basic Auth has been disabled in your environment.
4. Update all integrations to use supported methods (JWT, OAuth, SAML) per Oracle guidance.
5. Test all APIs to validate they function correctly under the new authentication method.

check.check-content:
1. Review your Service Request history with Oracle to confirm a request has been submitted to disable Basic Auth for APIs.
2. Confirm Oracle’s response/documentation showing that Basic Auth is disabled in the environment.
3. Attempt API calls using Basic Authentication and verify they fail.
4. Use supported authentication (JWT, SAML, OAuth) to confirm the API works with secure methods.

Rule.title: Ensure All API Based Integrations Use OAuth Authentication
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>All API based integrations with Oracle SaaS Applications must use OAuth 2.0 authentication configured through the Fusion Identity Domain. Basic Authentication, long-lived static passwords, or legacy authentication mechanisms must not be used for API or integration access. OAuth provides secure, token-based authentication with support for scopes, expiration, and revocation.

Rationale:
Basic Authentication and static credentials present significant risks, including credential theft, replay attacks, and the inability to enforce least-privilege access. Modern integrations require stronger controls to protect sensitive business transactions and data. Enforcing OAuth for all API and integration access aligns with industry standards and provides stronger security controls, including token expiration, scoped access, and easier revocation.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. Identify integrations currently using Basic Authentication by reviewing Fusion audit logs and OCI IAM authentication records.
2. Register OAuth clients in the Fusion Identity Domain for each integration, assigning only the required scopes and authorized resources.
3. Reconfigure integrations to use OAuth tokens in place of Basic Authentication credentials.
4. Disable or revoke Basic Authentication credentials in Fusion Applications and IAM domains.
5. Establish a recurring process to review Fusion and IAM logs to detect any attempted Basic Authentication use.

check.check-content:
1. Review all configured SOAP and REST integrations in Fusion Applications and Oracle Integration Cloud.
2. Confirm that integration clients are registered as OAuth clients in the Fusion Identity Domain and that Basic Authentication credentials are not in use.
3. Examine Fusion audit logs to identify API requests authenticated with Basic Authentication.
4. Review OCI IAM Identity Domain authentication logs to confirm that API access tokens are issued via OAuth flows only.
5. Validate that no unscoped or legacy credentials are present in active integrations.

Rule.title: Ensure Integration Account Secrets Are Rotated on a Regular Schedule
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Oracle SaaS environments often integrate with external systems using service accounts, OAuth clients, JWT signing keys, and X.509 certificates. These credentials are typically long-lived and, if not rotated regularly, may be compromised or reused by unauthorized parties. Organizations should enforce a policy to rotate all integration account secrets on a defined schedule, for example every 90 or 180 days, and update dependent integrations accordingly.

Rationale:
Long-lived credentials represent a significant risk if stolen, exposed in logs, or left unmanaged. Regular rotation reduces the risk window for credential misuse and aligns with best practices for key management. Scheduled rotation ensures that even if a secret is compromised, it cannot be abused indefinitely.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. Develop an inventory of all integration account secrets, including OAuth credentials, JWT keys, and certificates.
2. Define a rotation schedule (for example, 90 or 180 days) aligned with organizational policy and compliance requirements.
3. Rotate each credential according to the schedule, updating dependent integrations and notifying stakeholders.
4. Remove or revoke any unused or expired credentials to reduce the attack surface.
5. Document the process and maintain records of all credential rotations for audit purposes.

check.check-content:
1. Review integration accounts in Oracle Fusion Applications and identify all OAuth clients, JWT keys, and certificates in use.
2. Confirm that each credential has a documented rotation policy, including expiration and renewal dates.
3. Validate logs or change records to confirm that credentials have been rotated within the organization’s defined schedule (for example, within the past 180 days).
4. Check for expired or inactive credentials and confirm they are removed from production environments.

Rule.title: Ensure EPM Automate Credentials Are Protected via Secure Storage
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>EPM Automate requires credentials to execute commands such as data load, snapshot management, or audit log export. These credentials must never be stored in plaintext within scripts or configuration files. Instead, credentials must be secured using Oracle’ s encrypted password file (created with the encrypt command) or by integrating with secure enterprise credential vaults and OS-level key stores.

Rationale:
Storing credentials in plaintext exposes privileged accounts to theft and misuse. EPM Automate is commonly executed with Service Administrator-level rights, making it a high-value target. Using the encrypted password file or secure storage mechanisms significantly reduces the risk of credential exposure and aligns with security best practices.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
• Use the EPM Automate encrypt command to generate an encrypted password file and update scripts to reference it instead of plaintext arguments.
• Alternatively, configure integration with an enterprise password vault or OS secure key store to inject credentials at runtime.
• Regularly rotate credentials and regenerate encrypted storage files.
• Audit existing automation jobs to ensure compliance and remove any residual plaintext credentials.

check.check-content:
1. Review all automation scripts, scheduled jobs, and CI/CD processes invoking EPM Automate.
2. Verify that credentials are not stored in cleartext (e.g. in batch files, shell scripts, or parameters).
3. Confirm that either:
• The Oracle encrypted password file is being used, or
• Credentials are retrieved securely from an OS-level key store (e.g. Windows Credential Manager, Linux keyring) or an enterprise vault (e.g. CyberArk, HashiCorp Vault, OCI Vault).
4. Validate that credential rotation is in place and documented.

Rule.title: Ensure Dormant Accounts and Orphaned Identities Are Automatically Detected and Disabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Dormant accounts and orphaned identities should be detected and disabled using automated identity governance capabilities. Policies should be configured in OCI Identity Domains or integrated identity governance platforms to automatically flag and disable accounts that have not logged in within a defined period, or that have no role assignments or ownership.

Rationale:
Automated detection and disabling reduces reliance on manual reviews, minimizes human error, and ensures consistent enforcement. This strengthens the organization’s security posture and reduces the window of opportunity for account misuse.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. Implement identity governance tooling in OCI Identity Domains or an integrated IAM solution.
2. Configure policies to flag accounts inactive for more than 90 days or lacking ownership/role assignments.
3. Set policies to disable such accounts automatically while notifying administrators.
4. Define exceptions for service accounts and apply compensating monitoring controls.
5. Periodically review policy effectiveness and adjust thresholds as needed.

check.check-content:
1. Verify that identity governance policies are configured to automatically detect dormant and orphaned accounts.
2. Review policy logs to confirm detection and disabling actions have occurred.
3. Check for exceptions or exclusions and validate that they are documented and approved.

Rule.title: Ensure Dormant Accounts and Orphaned Identities Are Reviewed and Disabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Dormant accounts and orphaned identities should be identified and disabled on a regular schedule. Dormant accounts are active accounts that have not been used for a defined period, such as 90 days. Orphaned identities are accounts with no associated owner or role assignment. Manual reviews of account activity in Fusion Applications and OCI Identity Domains should be conducted at least quarterly to detect such accounts.

Rationale:
Inactive or orphaned accounts present unnecessary risk, as they may still be accessible but not actively monitored. Regular reviews reduce the chance that attackers exploit forgotten accounts to gain unauthorized access.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. Establish a policy defining thresholds for dormant accounts (for example, 90 days inactivity).
2. Schedule quarterly reports of user activity and ownership.
3. Review results with application owners.
4. Disable or delete dormant and orphaned accounts once confirmed unnecessary.
5. Document results and keep evidence for audit purposes.

check.check-content:
1. Generate user activity reports for Fusion Applications or OCI Identity Domains.
2. Identify accounts with no sign-in activity for at least 90 days.
3. Identify accounts without assigned roles, groups, or owners.
4. Confirm that such accounts are reviewed and, if appropriate, disabled or removed.

Rule.title: Ensure Network Perimeters are Configured in IAM or the Identity Provider
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Network Perimeters restrict where users can sign in to Oracle SaaS applications by enforcing trusted IP ranges or network sources. For upgraded environments, this is configured natively in Oracle Identity Domains. For environments that have not yet been upgraded, equivalent controls should be configured in the external identity provider (IdP).

Rationale:
Restricting access to approved IPs or network locations at the identity layer reduces the risk of compromised credentials being used from untrusted or malicious networks. By placing the enforcement at the authentication layer, even valid credentials cannot be misused outside authorized locations.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. Upgraded environments (OCI IAM):
• Go to Identity & Security, Domains, Security, Network Perimeters.
• Create a perimeter with approved IP ranges.
• Attach the perimeter to sign-on policies.
2. Non-upgraded environments (external IdP):
• Configure conditional access rules in the IdP (Azure AD, Okta, etc.).
• Define approved IP ranges or geolocation-based conditions.
• Apply these rules to authentication policies used by Oracle SaaS.

check.check-content:
1. For upgraded environments:
• Sign in to the Oracle Cloud Console.
• Navigate to Identity & Security, Domains, Security, Network Perimeters.
• Verify that at least one Network Perimeter is defined with authorized IP ranges and attached to sign-on policies.
2. For non-upgraded environments:
• Review conditional access or equivalent policies in the IdP.
• Confirm that rules are applied to restrict authentication attempts to approved IP ranges or network locations.

Rule.title: Ensure OCI Console Access Is Restricted to Trusted Networks
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that access to the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Console is restricted to trusted networks (secure VPNs or private network endpoints) by configuring IAM Network Sources

Rationale:
The OCI Console provides administrative access. If user credentials are compromised, unrestricted access from any IP address increases the attack surface. Restricting console login to approved IP ranges or VCN subnets enforces defense in depth and reduces the likelihood of unauthorized access.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. Define a Network Source with trusted IP ranges or VCN subnets:
• Navigate to Identity & Security, Network Sources, Create Network Source.
• Add approved IPs or CIDRs.
2. Update the Sign-On Policy for the identity domain:
• Add a rule that allows console login only if request.networkSource.name matches the trusted network source.
• Add a default deny rule for all other networks.
3. Test access from both inside and outside the trusted network.
4. Maintain a secure break-glass account exempt from the restriction.

check.check-content:
1. Navigate to Identity & Security, Domains, Security, Sign-On Policies.
• Confirm that console login rules reference a defined network source (for example, request.networkSource.name = <TrustedSource>).
• Verify that there is no policy rule permitting console access from any network.
2. Navigate to Identity & Security, Network Sources.
• Confirm that the trusted network source contains only approved IP addresses, CIDR blocks, or VCN subnets.

Rule.title: Ensure Access to Fusion is restricted via Access Control List
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>An Access Control List (ACL) restricts connections to Oracle Fusion SaaS environments by allowing access only from defined public IP addresses, CIDR ranges, or Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Virtual Cloud Networks (VCNs). This ensures that access is limited to approved enterprise networks and private connectivity options such as FastConnect or VPN, while blocking all other traffic by default.

Rationale:
Enabling ACLs enforces strict network perimeter controls around Oracle Fusion environments. By limiting access to trusted IPs or VCNs, ACLs protect against unauthorized access attempts from the public internet and reduce the risk of brute force, credential stuffing, and other network-based attacks. ACLs also align with zero-trust principles by ensuring SaaS applications are not broadly exposed.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content: 1. In the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Console, access the Fusion SaaS environment’s network configuration 2. Enable the Access Control List feature if not already active 3. Add the organization’s trusted public IP addresses, CIDR ranges, and/or OCI Virtual Cloud Networks (VCNs) to the ACL 4. Save the configuration and confirm that the ACL is enforced 5. Remove any broad or unnecessary ranges that could allow access from untrusted sources 6. Document any exceptions that must remain open, including justification and approval 7. Validate the changes by testing access from both allowed and disallowed networks to ensure enforcement is functioning as expected

check.check-content: 1. Sign in to the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Console with the appropriate administrator privileges 2. Navigate to the Fusion SaaS environment’s network settings and locate the Access Control List configuration 3. Verify that ACLs are enabled for the environment 4. Confirm that the ACL contains only trusted public IP addresses, CIDR ranges, or OCI Virtual Cloud Networks (VCNs) 5. Check that the allowlist excludes overly broad ranges such as 0.0.0.0/0 6. Validate that exceptions are documented and limited to approved use cases (for example, supplier portal or integrations that must be accessible from external networks) 7. Attempt access from an unlisted IP or VCN to confirm that connections are blocked

Rule.title: Ensure Location-Based Access Control (LBAC) is enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Location-Based Access Control (LBAC) restricts user access to Oracle Fusion SaaS products based on network location. It applies to both user interface (UI) and API sign- ins. Access is allowed only from registered IP ranges, such as corporate offices or VPN gateways. Users connecting from unregistered networks receive only generic or limited access unless explicitly permitted.

Rationale:
Enabling LBAC enforces a perimeter-based restriction on where users and integrations can connect from. This complements authentication and role-based authorization by ensuring that even valid credentials cannot be used from untrusted or malicious networks. Implementing LBAC reduces the attack surface and aligns with the principle of least privilege.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content: 1. Use an account with the IT Security Manager role to configure LBAC 2. In the Security Console, open the Location Based Access tab and select Enable Location Based Access 3. Add trusted IP addresses or CIDR ranges, including the administrator’s current IP to avoid lockout 4. Save the configuration and confirm the change 5. Mark the IT Security Manager role as public to preserve console access even from unregistered networks 6. If disabling LBAC, deselect the option; allowlist entries remain stored for reuse 7. Validate by testing login from both trusted and untrusted IPs

check.check-content: 1. Confirm that the IT Security Manager role is assigned 2. In a test or non-production environment, validate LBAC configuration before enabling in production 3. Navigate to Navigator, Tools, Security Console, Location Based Access 4. Verify that Enable Location Based Access is selected 5. Review the IP Address Allowlist to ensure it contains valid IPv4 or CIDR ranges for trusted networks 6. Confirm that the IT Security Manager role is designated as public to preserve administrative access 7. If LBAC is disabled, check that allowlist entries are retained in read-only mode for later use 8. Test login from a disallowed IP to confirm access is restricted, and from an allowed IP to confirm access works

Rule.title: Ensure Geolocation Filtering with WAF for SaaS is enforced
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Geolocation filtering in WAF for Oracle Fusion Applications restricts access based on the source country or region of incoming requests. WAF policies can be configured to allow or block traffic from selected geographies, helping organizations limit access to regions where legitimate users are located. This control must be enabled and validated through a Service Request with Oracle SaaS Operations.

Rationale:
Restricting access to only the countries or regions where the organization operates reduces unnecessary exposure to malicious traffic. Many automated attacks originate from outside business-relevant regions, and filtering them at the WAF layer prevents unwanted traffic from reaching the application.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. Submit a Service Request to Oracle SaaS Operations requesting geolocation filtering to be enabled for the Fusion environment.
2. Provide Oracle with the list of countries or regions that should be allowed or blocked.
3. After configuration by Oracle, confirm that the rules are applied and enforced.
4. Test by accessing Fusion from both allowed and blocked regions to ensure expected behavior.
5. Document exceptions if broader access must remain temporarily enabled.

check.check-content:
1. Review Service Request (SR) records with Oracle SaaS Operations to confirm that geolocation filtering has been enabled.
2. Verify the countries or regions included in the allow or block lists match organizational requirements.
3. Optionally log a new Service Request with Oracle SaaS Operations to confirm the current WAF policy configuration.
4. Validate functionality by attempting access from at least one blocked country and confirming that requests are denied.

Rule.title: Ensure IP-Based Filtering with WAF for SaaS is Enforced
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>IP-based filtering in WAF for Oracle Fusion Applications restricts access to trusted public IP addresses or CIDR ranges. WAF rules can allow or block specific IP ranges so that only authorized enterprise networks (such as corporate offices, VPN gateways, or partner networks) can reach Fusion Applications. This control must be enabled and validated through a Service Request with Oracle SaaS Operations.

Rationale:
Restricting access by IP address or CIDR reduces the exposure of Fusion Applications to unauthorized traffic from the public internet. By ensuring only trusted network sources can connect, IP-based filtering helps protect against brute force attempts, scanning, and other malicious activity.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. Submit a Service Request to Oracle SaaS Operations requesting IP-based filtering to be enabled for the Fusion environment.
2. Provide Oracle with a list of approved IP addresses or CIDR ranges representing trusted enterprise or VPN networks.
3. Review and approve Oracle’s implementation of the filtering policy.
4. Remove any unnecessary or overly broad ranges.
5. Validate enforcement by testing API and UI access from both allowed and disallowed IP addresses.
6. Document exceptions if temporary external access is required.

check.check-content:
1. Review Service Request (SR) records with Oracle SaaS Operations to confirm that IP-based filtering has been enabled.
2. Verify that the allowlist includes only approved public IP addresses or CIDR ranges corresponding to trusted networks.
3. Ensure no overly broad ranges, such as 0.0.0.0/0, are permitted.
4. Optionally log a Service Request with Oracle SaaS Operations to confirm the current WAF policy configuration.
5. Test connectivity from both an allowed and a disallowed IP address to confirm enforcement.

Rule.title: Ensure Qualified Target Filtering with WAF for SaaS is Enforced
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Qualified Target Filtering in WAF for Oracle Fusion Applications enables differentiated access control at the module or endpoint level. This allows organizations to apply stricter policies for sensitive internal modules while permitting broader access to externally facing modules, such as Supplier Portal and Oracle Recruiting Cloud Candidate Experience (ORC). Filtering rules can be defined per qualified target to separate external user traffic (e.g., suppliers, applicants) from internal corporate traffic.
This control must be enabled and validated through a Service Request with Oracle SaaS Operations.

Rationale:
Not all Fusion modules require the same level of exposure. Internal corporate modules should be tightly restricted, while external-facing portals must allow controlled access for third parties. Qualified Target Filtering provides the flexibility to enforce strong network restrictions for corporate use while preserving access for suppliers and applicants, minimizing unnecessary risk while supporting business functions.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. Submit a Service Request to Oracle SaaS Operations requesting Qualified Target Filtering to be enabled for the Fusion environment.
2. Provide Oracle with the list of Fusion modules requiring differentiated access (e.g., Supplier Portal, Candidate Experience) and their corresponding IP or geolocation restrictions.
3. Review Oracle’s implementation to ensure policies match business and security requirements.
4. Test access for both corporate and external traffic (supplier, applicant) to confirm correct behavior.
5. Document exceptions where broader access must be maintained.

check.check-content:
1. Review Service Request (SR) records with Oracle SaaS Operations to confirm that Qualified Target Filtering has been enabled.
2. Verify which Fusion modules are included in the configuration (e.g., Supplier Portal, Candidate Experience).
3. Review allowlist/blocklist rules applied to each qualified target (CIDR ranges, countries, or both).
4. Optionally log a Service Request with Oracle SaaS Operations to confirm the current Qualified Target Filtering policies.
5. Validate by testing access to each configured module from both allowed and disallowed IPs or regions to ensure differentiated enforcement.

Rule.title: Ensure Fusion Applications Login, Logout and Session Events are Captured, Exported, and Forwarded to Central Logging
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Capture all user authentication lifecycle events (successful and failed logins, logouts, session creation/termination, token refresh, and session invalidation) from Fusion Applications and ensure these events are exported to OCI Audit/Logging and forwarded to your centralized SIEM or log repository for retention, correlation, and alerting.
Sample alerts/detection rules:
• Multiple failed logins from same account or IP within short window.
• Login from new Geo-location or anonymized IP.
• Successful login immediately after password reset / privilege change.
• Concurrent sessions from geographically dispersed IPs for same user.

Rationale:
Authentication lifecycle events are fundamental telemetry for detecting account compromise, brute-force attacks, anomalous logins (time/location), and unauthorized session reuse. Centralizing these events enables correlation with other security data (privilege changes, API activity) and supports incident detection and forensic investigations.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

If using Oracle’s documented methods (REST API / Audit export), configure the export schedule and confirm delivery. 2.Establish ingestion pipeline: Create or verify t he Service Connector Hub (OCI Logging → Streaming → SIEM) or object -storage- based ingestion.

In the OCI Console 1. Verify Audit records (OCI Audit) capture high-level tenancy and console events.
For Fusion application session details, verify the tenant’s Fusion Audit export pipeline is configured, Confirm Fusion’s audit export is sending events to OCI Logging or to Object Storage.
2. In OCI Logging (or Object Storage), search for recent Fusion session events (examples: SignInSuccess, SignInFailure, SignOut, SessionCreated). Use query filters for eventName, principal, sourceIp, and eventTime.
3. Confirm the Service Connector Hub ingestion pipeline (Logging → Service Cconnector Hub, Streaming, or Object Storage ingestion) is operational and logs are flowing.

Rule.title: Ensure EPM Audit Data is Exported and Centrally Stored
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>EPM Cloud Applications generate audit data that records user sign-ins, administrative actions, and configuration changes. This audit data should be exported regularly from the EPM environment to ensure it is retained outside of the application. To ensure audit integrity and long-term availability, these audit records should be periodically exported from the service and stored in a centralized repository for example on Object Storage.

Rationale:
Audit data retained only inside EPM is limited by default retention policies and is vulnerable to loss or deletion. Exporting ensures durability and independence, while forwarding into OCI Logging Analytics or a SIEM enables consolidated monitoring, alerting, and compliance reporting across enterprise systems.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
• Configure automated export of EPM audit data (for example, with EPM Automate Access Log downloads).
• Store exported files securely outside the transactional environment.
• Test and validate that exports and any forwarding pipelines complete successfully, without data loss.

check.check-content:
1. Confirm that EPM audit data exports are scheduled and active.
2. Verify that audit data files contain expected details, such as user ID, login time, IP address, and executed functions.
3. Check that exported data is securely stored in an external location, like Object Storage.

Centralize this audit data for anomaly detection, insider-threat monitoring, and compliance reporting.

Rationale:
Reports and dashboards in Fusion Applications can access or export large volumes of sensitive operational and financial data. Auditing report execution and modification provides visibility into who viewed, changed, or extracted information, helping to prevent unauthorized disclosure or manipulation of analytics.
Usage metrics also provide early indicators of abuse or unusual access patterns.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure BPM Approval Rule and Workflow Configuration Changes Are Audited
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Enable and monitor auditing for changes to BPM (Business Process Management) approval rules and SOA workflow configurations within Oracle Fusion Applications.
These rules determine the routing and approval hierarchy for critical business transactions (e.g., expense approvals, journal entries, purchase orders, HR changes).
By auditing changes, organizations can maintain accountability for modifications that may alter segregation of duties or bypass established approval hierarchies.

Rationale:
Approval rules define key authorization paths that enforce financial and operational controls. Unauthorized or untracked changes can enable fraudulent approvals, insider threats, or policy violations. Auditing BPM/SOA configuration changes ensures the integrity and traceability of the enterprise approval model.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. Enable auditing for SOA/BPM components in Fusion’s audit configuration as per Doc ID 2053746.1.
2. Ensure all BPM rule changes are routed through change management or governance workflow.
3. Configure scheduled extraction of BPM audit logs for integration with centralized audit monitoring (OCI Logging, SIEM, or Analytics).
4. Implement periodic review (monthly/quarterly) of approval rule changes by business process owners and security administrators.
5. Set up alerts or dashboards for critical workflow-change events.

1. Access Setup and Maintenance → Manage Audit Policies → Audit Configuration.
2. Confirm that Audit for SOA/BPM Changes is Enabled (refer to Doc ID 2053746.1). Review Fusion Applications SOA Audit (Doc ID 2053746.1) 3. Verify that audit data is available through Audit Report / REST API.

Rule.title: Ensure Logging Pipelines are Monitored for Failures to Prevent Silent Loss of Audit Events
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Audit and monitoring data from Oracle SaaS Applications is often exported and ingested into downstream systems such as Centralized Log Management (CLM) or Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Platforms. If the export or ingestion pipelines fail, audit data may silently stop flowing, leaving security teams unaware of missing records. Monitoring and alerting should be enabled on all logging pipelines to detect failures and disruptions in log collection or forwarding.
In Oracle SaaS Connector Hub is the recommended log routing services. Organizations leveraging multi-cloud or hybrid environments may also use third-party log forwarding and observability agents to ensure reliable audit data delivery.

Rationale:
Audit data is critical for detecting malicious activity, ensuring accountability, and meeting compliance requirements. Pipeline failures can result in gaps that prevent accurate forensic investigations and weaken monitoring effectiveness. By actively monitoring the health of logging pipelines, organizations can ensure continuous visibility into user and administrative activity.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle SaaS Cloud Applications Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
1. Configure OCI Monitoring alarms on Service Connector Hub pipelines to trigger when ingestion or forwarding fails.
2. Establish alert rules in Centralized Log Management (CLM) or SIEM Platform to detect periods with no incoming audit events.
3. Route alarms to administrators via Notifications, email, or ticketing systems.
4. Test the monitoring setup by intentionally pausing or misconfiguring a pipeline and verifying that alerts are generated.
5. Document the monitoring and escalation process in the organization’s operational runbooks.

check.check-content:
1. If using OCI Service Connector Hub, open the OCI Console, review OCI Service Connector Hub to confirm monitoring is enabled on log collection and forwarding pipelines.
2. Check whether alarms exist in OCI Monitoring for connector errors, ingestion failures, or delivery delays.
3. Validate that alerts are directed to responsible administrators via email, pager, or incident management systems.
4. Inspect recent alarm history to confirm that test failures are detected and reported.

Rule.title: Ensure Changes to Audit Policy Settings Are Monitored
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The purpose of this recommendation is to ensure that changes to Audit Policies are appropriate. Audit Policies record the changes made to Fusion Application configuration settings, which in turn determine the applications' behaviors. Each Audit Policy records changes to specific settings. Administrators enable each Audit Policy separately. Once an Audit Policy is enabled, audit information is stored without any intervention of the user or any explicit user action. Administrators can also disable any Audit Policy separately - i.e., specify that specific settings' changes will no longer be recorded - and re-enable them later.

Rationale:
Changes to Audit Policies impact the ability to detect changes to Fusion Application configurations, and consequent changes to the applications' behaviors. This control ensures that changes are recorded, reviewed, and if necessary, reversed.
If an Audit Policy is disabled erroneously, the ability to monitor changes to Fusion Application configurations is lost; those changes will alter the applications' behaviors without appropriate oversight.
If an Audit Policy is disabled maliciously, Fusion Application configurations can be changed in unauthorized ways - a potential exploit is to disable an Audit Policy, change an application configuration setting, abuse the changed behavior of the application, then restore the original configuration setting and re-enable the Audit Policy.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>In Oracle EPM Cloud, you can enable pre-upload virus scanning using the setVirusScanOnFileUploads command so that files with malware are blocked before upload. In addition, enforce a file extension policy to restrict potentially dangerous file types (executables, scripts) from being uploaded.

Rationale:
Automatically scanning files before upload prevents malicious content from entering the environment. Combined with extension restrictions, this defense-in-depth approach reduces the risk from malware, ransomware, or embedded scripts being introduced via file upload.</VulnDiscussion>

• Test uploads to validate scanning and blocking is working as expected.
• Ensure that role assignment is controlled so only trusted Service Administrators can modify scan settings.
• Document exception handling (for business-justified file types) and apply compensating controls.
